## The big idea

At high Reynolds number, viscosity doesn't disappear — it **retreats into
a thin layer at the wall** and rules absolutely there. That layer grows
like $\sqrt{x}$ while laminar, transitions, then grows faster and drags
harder. Prandtl's 1904 insight — split the flow into a frictionless
outside and a viscous skin — rescued fluid mechanics from a century of
paradox and is the organizing idea of all external flow.

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: Re_x = ρUx/μ
The *local* Reynolds number, built on distance from the leading edge —
so it grows as the flow travels. Below ~5×10⁵: laminar layer. Beyond:
transition to turbulence *on the same surface*. One plate, two regimes,
position decides.
:::

## The reconciliation

Here is the paradox Prandtl resolved. At high Re, N–S says viscosity is
negligible (Unit 6's own scaling) — and frictionless theory then predicts
**zero drag** on a body, which is absurd (d'Alembert knew it was absurd
in 1752). But viscosity *can't* be negligible at the wall: no-slip pins
the fluid to zero there while the free stream roars by at $U$, and that
velocity contrast must be bridged somewhere. Prandtl's move: it's bridged
in a layer so thin that the outer flow never notices it — yet inside it,
velocity gradients are enormous, the viscous term is fully in charge, and
all the friction of the flow is manufactured.

**Why $\sqrt{x}$?** Recall 6.1: momentum diffuses like heat, with
diffusivity $\nu = \mu/\rho$. The wall's "message" (*you must stop*)
spreads outward by diffusion — distance $\sim\sqrt{\nu t}$ — while the
flow carries the message downstream at $U$, so a station $x$ has been
exposed for $t = x/U$:

$$\delta \sim \sqrt{\nu\, x / U} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\delta}{x} \sim \frac{5.0}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Re}_x}} \; \text{(laminar, with the exact constant)}.$$

Run the numbers and the layer is startlingly thin: air at 30 m/s, one
meter along a surface — Re_x = 2×10⁶, and the laminar formula would give
δ ≈ 3.5 mm. *Millimeters*, on a meter of car roof. Thin — but 100% of
the skin friction lives inside it, and its behavior decides whether the
flow stays attached at all (7.2's stakes).

**Transition.** As the layer thickens downstream, its own local Reynolds
number grows until, near $\mathrm{Re}_x \approx 5\times10^5$ (sooner with
roughness, turbulence, vibration — the number is a lab value, not a law),
the layer trips into turbulence. The turbulent layer mixes momentum far
faster than molecular diffusion, so it grows faster ($\sim x^{0.8}$),
sits *blunter* against the wall — and you know from 6.2 exactly what
blunt-at-the-wall means: steeper slope, more shear, **more drag**. Watch
all of it happen on one plate:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof U_71 = Inputs.range([1, 60], {value: 15, step: 1, label: "free-stream U (m/s), air"})
viewof L_71 = Inputs.range([0.3, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "plate length (m)"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - U_71
#|   - L_71
nu = 1.5e-5
x = np.linspace(1e-4, L_71, 400)
d = np.array([delta(xi, U_71, nu) for xi in x])
cf = np.array([cf_local(U_71*xi/nu) for xi in x])
x_tr = 5e5*nu/U_71
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.2), sharex=True)
ax1.plot(x, d*1000, lw=2.5)
ax1.set_ylabel('δ (mm)')
ax2.plot(x, cf*1000, lw=2.5, color='darkorange')
ax2.set_ylabel('c_f × 1000'); ax2.set_xlabel('x along plate (m)')
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    if x_tr < L_71:
        ax.axvline(x_tr, color='crimson', ls='--', lw=1.2)
if x_tr < L_71:
    ax1.annotate(f' transition at x = {x_tr:.2f} m', (x_tr, d.max()*0.55),
                 color='crimson', fontsize=9)
    ax1.set_title(f"δ at the trailing edge: {d[-1]*1000:.1f} mm — and the layer restarts thicker & hungrier")
else:
    ax1.set_title(f"entirely laminar (Re_L = {U_71*L_71/nu:,.0f}) — δ ends at {d[-1]*1000:.1f} mm")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Two things to make yourself see. The **jump at the dashed line**: at
transition, thickness leaps and — look at the lower panel — the local
friction roughly *quadruples*, then decays more slowly than before. And
the **leading edge**: $c_f$ is enormous there (the layer is thinnest, the
gradient fiercest) — fresh surfaces are expensive surfaces, which is why
7.2's mixed-plate drag formula weights the front of a body so heavily.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
δ is not "where the flow stops" and the boundary layer is not stagnant
fluid stuck to the wall. It's the (conventionally 99%-of-U) zone where
the velocity climbs from zero to the free stream — fluid inside it moves
briskly and streams downstream. Nor is thin the same as ignorable: the
millimeters at the wall set the drag of ships, the range of aircraft, and
(next module) whether the flow stays attached at all.
:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** Same speed, water instead of air. Is the boundary layer on the plate thicker or thinner?</summary>
Thinner — δ ∼ √(νx/U) and water's kinematic viscosity is ~15× *smaller*
than air's (its μ is bigger, but its ρ is bigger still). Momentum
diffuses more sluggishly through water, so the wall's message spreads
less far.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Where on a 3 m car roof at highway speed is the boundary layer laminar?</summary>
Almost nowhere: x_tr = 5×10⁵ν/U ≈ 5×10⁵ × 1.5×10⁻⁵/30 ≈ 0.25 m — the
first hand-span, at best, and real-world roughness usually trips it
sooner. Practical external flows are overwhelmingly turbulent-layer
flows; the laminar formulas earn their keep on small, slow, smooth things.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Why does the *turbulent* layer resist separation better (a teaser this module owes 7.2)?</summary>
Its mixing continually imports fast fluid down toward the wall, so the
near-wall region carries more momentum — a fuller wallet for pushing
through an adverse pressure gradient before the 6.2 diagnosis (zero wall
slope) arrives. Golf balls are dimpled to buy exactly this.
</details>

## Bring to class

Estimate — order of magnitude, no calculator ceremony — δ at the trailing
edge of: a dragonfly wing, a kayak, a container ship. Bring the three
numbers; we'll argue about which regime each layer is in.
